questions.prompt: What does dominant-pole compensation do to an op-amp?
options: It removes all poles above DC
It raises the gain at high frequency to widen the bandwidth
It makes the op-amp's DC gain infinite
It adds or moves one pole to a low frequency, so the gain falls to 1 before the next pole adds much phase lag
questions.explanation:
With one dominant pole, the open-loop phase sits near \(-90^\circ\) over most of the band. As long as the second pole lies above the unity-gain frequency, every feedback configuration keeps a healthy phase margin. The cost is bandwidth: the gain starts rolling off very early.
• Poles cannot be removed, only placed.
• Raising the high-frequency gain would push the crossover toward the second pole and reduce the margin.
• Compensation does not change the DC gain.

questions.prompt: Why is the unity-gain follower (\(f=1\)) the hardest configuration to keep stable?
options: It has the largest feedback factor, so \(|T|=|A|\) crosses 1 at the highest frequency, closest to the op-amp's second pole
Its closed-loop gain is lowest, and low gain is always unstable
It has no feedback resistors to add damping
Its output swing is largest
questions.explanation:
The loop gain is \(T=Af\). With \(f=1\), the crossover happens where \(|A|=1\), at the unity-gain frequency, where the op-amp's higher poles add the most phase lag. With \(f=0.1\) the crossover drops to where \(|A|=10\), a decade lower, and the margin improves. 'Unity-gain stable' op-amps are compensated for this worst case.
• Low closed-loop gain is not unstable by itself; it is the large f that matters.
• Resistors do not supply damping in this sense.
• Output swing is unrelated to small-signal stability.

questions.prompt: A follower uses an op-amp modeled as \(A(s)=\dfrac{\omega_u}{s}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1+s/\omega_{p2}}\) with \(f_u=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\) and a second pole at \(f_{p2}=3\ \mathrm{MHz}\). What is the phase margin, in degrees?
questions.explanation:
Crossover: \(\dfrac{f_u}{f}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+(f/f_{p2})^2}}=1\), which gives \(f_c=0.95\ \mathrm{MHz}\). The phase there is \(-90^\circ-\tan^{-1}(0.95/3)=-107.6^\circ\), so PM \(=72.4^\circ\).
• \(90-\tan^{-1}(1/3)=71.6^\circ\) uses \(f_u\) as the crossover, a close approximation.
• 90° ignores the second pole.
• \(-107.6^\circ\) is the phase itself, not the margin.
questions.figure_alt: Follower loop gain: falling 20 dB per decade through 0 dB near 1 MHz, steepening after 3 MHz.

questions.prompt: An op-amp is stable as a gain-of-10 amplifier but oscillates when connected as a unity-gain follower. Why?
options: Because the follower has no feedback
Because the follower's gain of 1 means \(T=1\) at all frequencies
With \(f=1\) the loop gain \(T=Af\) is 10× larger, so the crossover moves up toward the non-dominant poles and the phase margin shrinks
Because lower closed-loop gain always gives MORE phase margin, so this can't happen
questions.explanation:
\(T=A(j\omega)f\): raising \(f\) from 0.1 to 1 lifts the whole \(|T|\) curve by 20 dB, so the unity crossing moves from \(\approx f_u/10\) to \(\approx f_u\), closer to the extra poles. The follower is the hardest case, which is why datasheets advertise 'unity-gain stable' op-amps.
Gotcha: low closed-loop gain means HIGH loop gain, and less margin.

questions.prompt: For the same follower model (\(f_u=2\ \mathrm{MHz}\)), where must the second pole \(f_{p2}\) be to get exactly 60° of phase margin, in MHz?
questions.explanation:
PM \(=90^\circ-\tan^{-1}(f_c/f_{p2})=60^\circ\) requires \(f_c=f_{p2}\tan30^\circ=0.577f_{p2}\). Crossover means \(\dfrac{f_u}{f_c}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+1/3}}=1\), so \(f_c=0.866f_u=1.73\ \mathrm{MHz}\) and \(f_{p2}=1.73/0.577=3.0\ \mathrm{MHz}=1.5f_u\).
• \(f_u\tan60^\circ=3.46\ \mathrm{MHz}\) assumes the crossover stays at \(f_u\).
• 2 MHz (\(f_{p2}=f_u\)) gives only about 52°.

questions.prompt: Miller compensation puts a capacitor across an inverting gain stage inside the op-amp. Besides lowering the dominant pole, what does it do to the output-stage pole?
options: It moves the output pole lower, next to the dominant pole
It pushes the output pole to a higher frequency (pole splitting), which improves the phase margin further
It cancels the output pole exactly
It has no effect on the output pole
questions.explanation:
The Miller capacitor's feedback lowers the impedance at the output node at high frequency, so the second pole moves up as the first moves down. The poles 'split' apart, which is what makes a single small on-chip capacitor so effective.
• Moving both poles together would worsen the margin.
• There is no exact cancellation; that would need a matched zero.
• The effect on the output pole is the point of the technique.

questions.prompt: An op-amp has \(A(jf)=\dfrac{10^5}{(1+jf/10\ \mathrm{Hz})(1+jf/2\ \mathrm{MHz})}\) (\(f_u\approx1\ \mathrm{MHz}\)). Connected as a follower (\(f=1\)), what is the phase margin? Solve \(|T|=1\) numerically.
questions.explanation:
\(T=A\). Solving \(|A(jf)|=1\): \(f_c=910.2\ \mathrm{kHz}\) (a bit below 1 MHz because the second pole already bends the curve).
\(\angle T=-\tan^{-1}(f_c/10)-\tan^{-1}(f_c/2\ \mathrm{MHz})\approx-90^\circ-24.5^\circ\), so PM \(=65.5^\circ\).
With \(f=0.1\) the crossover drops to \(\approx100\ \mathrm{kHz}\) and PM \(\approx87^\circ\): same op-amp, very different margin.

questions.prompt: A follower (\(f_u=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\), otherwise ideal dominant-pole op-amp) has open-loop output resistance \(R_o=50\ \Omega\) and drives \(C_L=10\ \mathrm{nF}\). The load adds a pole at \(1/(2\pi R_oC_L)\). What is the phase margin, in degrees?
questions.explanation:
The load pole is at \(1/(2\pi\cdot50\cdot10\ \mathrm{nF})=318\ \mathrm{kHz}\), well below \(f_u\). The crossover falls to about 0.52 MHz, where the phase is \(-90^\circ-\tan^{-1}(0.52/0.318)\approx-148.6^\circ\), so PM is about 31.4°. Large capacitive loads are a classic cause of follower ringing.
• About 72° would need the load pole above \(f_u\).
• 90° ignores the load.
questions.figure_alt: Follower loop gain with a capacitive-load pole: the slope steepens to 40 dB per decade before 0 dB.

questions.prompt: A designer puts a small isolation resistor \(R_{iso}\) between the op-amp's output and a large capacitive load, and takes the feedback from the op-amp side of \(R_{iso}\). Why does this help?
options: It increases the op-amp's DC gain
It removes the load capacitance from the circuit
Seen from the feedback point, the load is now an RC network that adds a zero next to the load pole, giving back phase near crossover
It lowers the unity-gain frequency to DC
questions.explanation:
\(R_{iso}\) in series with \(C_L\) adds a zero at \(1/(R_{iso}C_L)\), which cancels much of the load pole's phase lag near crossover, so the margin recovers. The price is a small DC error or slower settling at the load node.
• DC gain is unchanged.
• The capacitor is still there; only its effect on the loop is softened.
• \(f_u\) does not move.

questions.prompt: Preview of capacitive loads. A follower's op-amp (\(A\approx f_u/jf\), \(f_u=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\)) has \(R_{out}=100\ \Omega\) and drives \(C_L=4.7\ \mathrm{nF}\). The load adds a pole at \(1/(2\pi R_{out}C_L)\). What is the phase margin? Solve \(|T|=1\) numerically.
questions.explanation:
Load pole: \(f_{p2}=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\cdot100\ \Omega\cdot4.7\ \mathrm{nF}}=0.339\ \mathrm{MHz}\). With \(T=\dfrac{f_u}{jf}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1+jf/f_{p2}}\), \(|T|=1\) at \(f_c=534.9\ \mathrm{kHz}\).
\(\angle T=-90^\circ-\tan^{-1}(f_c/f_{p2})\), so PM \(=32.3^\circ\): below the 60° target. Common-source stages with big capacitive loads face the same pole.

questions.prompt: Preview of compensation. A follower's loop gain is \(T=\dfrac{f_u}{jf}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1+jf/f_{p2}}\) with a non-dominant pole \(f_{p2}=10\ \mathrm{MHz}\). Dominant-pole compensation sets \(f_u\). Which \(f_u\) puts the crossover exactly at \(f_{p2}\) (phase margin \(45^\circ\)), in MHz?
questions.explanation:
At \(f=f_{p2}\): \(|T|=\dfrac{f_u}{f_{p2}}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=1\Rightarrow f_u=\sqrt2\,f_{p2}=14.14\ \mathrm{MHz}\).
For 60° you would need \(f_u\) lower still. Designers lower \(f_u\) by enlarging the dominant capacitance, often with the Miller effect, which is coming soon.

questions.prompt: Preview of compensation. The follower driving \(C_L\) has too little phase margin. Using only stability ideas, which change helps?
options: Lower the op-amp's \(f_u\) (more dominant-pole compensation), so the crossover moves well below the load pole
Increase \(C_L\) further
Raise \(f_u\) so the loop is faster
Increase the feedback factor beyond 1
questions.explanation:
Phase margin improves when the crossover sits far below the non-dominant pole. Lowering \(f_u\) moves the crossover down. A larger \(C_L\) moves the load pole DOWN (worse). Raising \(f_u\) pushes the crossover up into the pole (worse). \(f\) can't exceed 1 with a passive network.
Miller compensation is the classic way to lower \(f_u\) on-chip.
